packs.title: Across the City
packs.promise: Explore tower structures, museum objects and open landscapes across Kuala Lumpur.

q.s: Collect design details that make a city pause easier.
st: Follow an open path until you can observe a patterned walking surface, a shaded edge or shelter, and a place to rest. Leave each feature in place.

Make a small comfort kit in your notes: describe the surface underfoot, what makes shade here, and how the resting place faces the park. Use the visible feature rather than a guessed design intention.
Choose the detail that would help you stay longest on a warm day. Explain your choice using what you observed.

q.s: Move at your own pace and map one useful turning point.
st: Choose a currently open main path near the garden’s lake or a planted area. Pick a comfortable outward interval, up to 10 minutes; a shorter interval earns the same credit.
Travel at your own pace, then turn back at a visible landmark such as a path junction, shelter or lake view. Stop before checking your phone.
Make a route note with your start, turning landmark and one place where shade or the surface changed your pace. Describe the route you actually used, not an assumed complete lake loop.

q.s: Pause with a reflection and notice what changes.
st: Choose a comfortable public viewpoint set back from the water and out of the walking lane. Sit or stand as suits you.
Watch the same small part of the lake for a few minutes. Notice a reflection or patch of light that moves, and a shoreline or distant shape that remains steadier.
Write one sentence for the change and one for what stayed. A quiet or cloudy view still works; there is no required skyline, fountain or wildlife sighting.

packs.title: Squares, Craft and Chinatown
packs.promise: Explore the connected civic district and Chinatown through public spaces, craft and visitor galleries.

q.s: Let an exterior shape set the pace of a short piece of writing.
st: Stop on the public pavement where you can see an exterior door or window and a roof edge. Choose two clear lines or shapes in the façade.
Write two original lines about the actual exterior: make the first short and precise, and let the second stretch along the larger shape you chose. A small drawing with two written labels also works.
Read your work once and revise one word or edge so that a visitor could recognise the feature you used. Do not invent an interior detail or a story about someone connected with the church.

q.s: Turn a public clock-tower outline into your own route keepsake.
st: From a stopped public viewpoint, choose one visible geometric shape from the clock tower and a different edge or pattern from a surrounding façade.

On your own paper or in text, make a clock for your afternoon. Use those shapes to arrange three moments from the route you have actually experienced; these are your memory markers, not facts about the tower’s hands.
Add a short explanation of which shape came from which exterior feature. Keep the work with you and leave the square unchanged.

q.s: Follow a real market corridor and map where your pace changes.
st: Start at an open public end or section of the market corridor. Identify your starting landmark from a street sign or a visible entrance feature.
Move at a comfortable pace through the open corridor, stopping clear of the flow where the space becomes wider, narrower or more sheltered. Notice how the layout changes your own movement.
Draw a small route or write a before-and-after note with your actual start and finish. Include one point where the street’s layout changed your pace, without making assumptions about other people.
